speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious matter. Recognizing its seriousness, we on this side feel it should be discussed in the house at this time. We feel very strongly that the situation which now prevails on the Montreal docks has been brought about by the ineptness of this government in dealing with the matter.
I want to refer back to July of last year, specifically to July 14, 1966, when the government introduced Bill No. C-215, an act respecting certain conditions of employment of dock workers at the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec. This bill was discussed on that day and we pointed out to the
DEBATES	4651
Labour Dispute at Montreal government the error it was making in taking that step. We objected in particular to the preamble to the bill, part of which read as follows:
And whereas an industrial inquiry commission to inquire into those certain matters has been appointed under the said act, and it is in the national interest that the conclusions of the said commission with respect thereto be carried into effect without delay following receipt of the report of the said commission-
I pointed out during the debate on the bill, Mr. Speaker, that this was contrary to the collective bargaining arguments that the government has always hidden behind. As recorded at page 7674 of Hansard for July 14, 1966 I said:
A commissioner can be appointed. No one will object to that. The commissioner can go to work and eventually, upon hearing both sides and investigating the situation completely, he can make a report to the Minister of Labour who in turn should refer that report to the interested parties as a basis for collective bargaining.
The government ignored this suggestion, even though the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), the next speaker for the New Democratic party, agreed that this was the proper procedure to take.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has happened? A report has been made by the commissioner of inquiry, Mr. Picard. This report was made to the Minister of Labour. Did the Minister of Labour feel there should be ample opportunity for the interested parties in the dispute to sit down with him or to consult amongst themselves before the report was implemented, to see whether they would interpret the report in the same way and agree on what should be done? No; the minister arbitrarily imposed the report on both parties without reference to them at all.
We now have a situation where the parties interpret the report differently. One party reads it one way and the other party reads it another way. Consequently there is a tie-up in the port of Montreal, where some 40 ships are standing idle waiting to be unloaded. Fruits, vegetables and other commodities of this country are being allowed to rot while the government sits quietly by contending that someone else should see that this national crisis is resolved.
I know the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Martin) has a tremendous responsibility and is trying to show his concern for the country. Surely in his wisdom he could prevail on the Minister of Labour and ask him to forgo his obstinate, arrogant attitude that the government is not responsible and that it is up to
4652	COMMONS
Labour Dispute at Montreal someone else to decide what is to be done. The government in this crisis surely has a responsibility to rectify the situation at once.
We said the legislation was based on an assumption; how were we to know what the report would be? How could we agree to that report being imposed as part of the collective bargaining agreement? We voted against this bill because of that. On page 7674 of Hansard for July 14, 1966 I am reported to have said:
This legislation is based on assumption. The government is assuming that the recommendations will be acceptable to both parties.
The recommendations are not acceptable to both parties, and we were right. Continuing:
What will be the situation if the recommendations are not acceptable?
We have that situation now. There is chaos on the Montreal docks, and that chaos will probably spread across the country to other docks. The union members will not sit idly by and see this type of recommendation imposed on their fellow members. Sympathetic gestures by other union members will be made, as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration well knows. Continuing to quote, I am reported to have said:
Will that tend to a happy and harmonious situation between these two parties for the duration of the present agreement?
There is no happy and harmonious situation which at that time the government thought there would be. Continuing:
This is almost prophetic legislation. We do not know what is going to be recommended but we are being asked to put unknown recommendations into effect.
After that warning the government, on receipt of the report, without consulting both sides as is the normal practice under collective agreements, imposed an arbitrary piece of legislation. Surely that was the most arbitrary decision that could have been taken. I say the present crisis on the Montreal waterfront arises directly from that legislation which the government passed on July 15. Consequently I and many others feel that the government has a responsibility in this situation, but the government does not accept that.
In the legislation the government imposed on unions and management the terms of the Picard report, which then had not been written. In July 1966, during the debate, we were assured by the Minister of Labour and the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration that the unwritten recommendations of

By its mismanagement the government in this instance has occasioned the spoilage of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of goods. I mention this because I wish to show the insubstantial and contradictory nature of the minister's position. He cannot be allowed his attitude of being almost a hundred light years away from what is taking place on the Montreal docks. Yesterday I asked him whether he would assume the responsibility of calling both parties to Ottawa at once to try to bring about some understanding and acceptance of this report. That is all that can be done in the circumstances. The government cannot sit idly by and allow events to develop without taking action. Calling the parties to Ottawa for consultation is the only reasonable and the only responsible approach the government should take at this time. After all, they introduced the bill and imposed the terms of the report.
At the time the bill was passed the union had never agreed to the incredible proposal of accepting something which was as then unwritten. Nevertheless the government went ahead, and it went ahead without the agreement of the union or management. The government shoved the bill through and we voted against it. The government have a responsibility to act, and they must exercise that responsibility.
I wish the Acting Prime Minister would not adopt a light hearted attitude and smile. The situation is most serious.

welcome this opportunity to discuss the important question now before the house. We believe the work stoppage will do incalculable harm to the whole of the Canadian economy. The immediate pressure arises in connection with the perishable merchandise to which the mover of the motion has already referred, but we are so close to the end of the shipping season in Montreal that the cost of this stoppage to the Canadian ecoonmy, if it continues, is something which cannot be calculated.

There is no authority under which the Minister of Labour can intervene in cases of this kind. The parties must learn they should try to work out their own differences.
I personally have always said that free collective bargaining means negotiation between labour and management, and that governments cannot and should not intervene in every dispute. But consider the circumstances in this case. Here is a stoppage which is taking place because the government of Canada did intervene at an earlier stage. Last year when there were problems and stoppages the government of Canada put
Labour Dispute at Montreal forward legislation with which many of us disagreed violently. It put forward legislation appointing an arbitrator and making it a condition of the law that the award of the arbitrator should be binding on both parties. It is as a result of that legislation and of an award by Mr. Picard, the wording of which is apparently unacceptable to either side, that we are faced with this stoppage.
It is not a sudden or an unexpected stoppage. For weeks the signs have been apparent. For weeks it has been obvious from press reports, messages and telegrams from the union to representatives of the various parties in this house, that all was not going well. I am sure the shipping federation has been in communication with the minister for some time. For weeks it has been obvious that the arbitration award was giving rise to difficulty, that the understanding of both parties as to its meaning was different. It was obvious that there would be trouble.
The union claims the companies are implementing only those portions of the award which suit them. I shall not go into details, but as I understand it one of the major sections of the arbitration decision provided that there should be a reduction in the number of people working in each gang. The arbitrator obviously based this part of the award on the fact that with the use of more modern equipment the work could be done by gangs containing fewer men than in the past. I believe the number of men was cut from 21 to 16. This is a sharp decrease but, as I understand it, the union and the men are not disputing this decision. They recognize that the advance of technology cannot and should not be stopped.
However, as I understand their case they take the position that in return for agreeing to this reduction in the size of the work force the award contained provision for certain guarantees in connection with the minimum hours for which the men would be paid each week, and so on. As I understand the position the companies have refused to implement this part of the arbitration award. Under these conditions, believing that the companies are unfairly using the law passed by parliament and using unfairly an award made by an arbitrator, and faced by the refusal of the companies to discuss these matters in any kind of amicable and open minded way, the union and the men have resorted to work stoppages.
To me it seems obvious that since the dispute has arisen as a result of differences of opinion as to the report of an arbitrator

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot for moving the adjournment motion. What we are engaged in is our annual exercise in attempting to free the flow of exports through our dock facilities. We have not quite landed on the anniversary of the last time the business of the house was adjourned to discuss a dock tie up, but we are only a week away from it. This means that an entire year has elapsed during which legislation could have been introduced to deal with this area of the economy, legislation which would have been more than a patchwork solution to an immediate problem and which would have provided some different means of settling this sort of dispute that would not involve the disruption of the flow of exports.
We can expect that if such legislation is not introduced during the coming year then in exactly one year's time, give or take a day or two, we shall be engaged in this same exercise. It seems that annually we pass legislation to deal with emergency situations, to get goods flowing again, but we do not compensate industries thousands of miles away from the work stoppages that suffer not only in the immediate year of the stoppage but in successive years, due to lost markets caused by lack of confidence in the ability of those industries to move their goods on time.
I would use the same example I used a year ago. I have received the same sort of telegram that I received a year ago. The only difference in this case is that the east coast ports are substituted for the west coast ports. I realize that the dispute itself is of a slightly different nature, but the effect on the particular industry in my province, my con-stituencey, is exactly the same. Such a situation as this produces in that industry, and I am sure in hundreds of others clear across the country, an absolutely scalding frustration at the inability of this parliament to move effectively to prevent this becoming the annual occurrence that we all know it has become.
Looking at the example of the fruit industry in British Columbia, I would point out
November 24, 1987	COMMONS
that this year import restrictions in the United Kingdom were eased for the first time in many years. This meant a larger market than usual available to an industry whose export markets are absolutely vital. In this context we must look at the things which have happened in rapid confusion over the last few weeks.
The pound sterling has been devalued. While this may not have an immediate impact on the export market this year, the future implications are very serious. In addition a surcharge has been imposed on freight rates from the St. Lawrence ports, a very significant surcharge of 25 per cent clear across the board on all goods moving through those ports, because of the frustration of the shippers who have learned that they cannot move goods freely through those ports. On top of that we have had virtually a complete shutdown of the docks, as a result of which goods that have already moved to the port of Montreal for shipment are in danger of spoiling there before they reach market. The implications for the future are very great.
I sympathize with the minister in the statement he made yesterday, when he suggested that both sides to the dispute act responsibly and use the grievance procedure available to them and attempt to make it work. But we realize that by means of a great variety of legislation during the last several years we have been engaged in the process of chipping away at individual and private responsibility in many fields. We have now reached the point where we cannot expect a prompt and decisive result to spring from the minister's hopes, hopes with which I have every sympathy.

Our group would have preferred it if the debate had originated on the other side of the house, and I think that the minister should have taken the opportunity yesterday or today to make an important statement on the present circumstances in the Montreal harbour.

summer of 1966. The collective agreements between the shipping federation and the longshoremen in the St. Lawrence ports had expired on December 31, 1965. The parties had some discussions and in April, 1966 they asked for the establishment of a conciliation board. The minister has not only the right but the duty to establish a conciliation board when such action is requested. Within a matter of hours of the time that request was received a conciliation board was established. On the very day that the representative of management and the representative of the workers asked for the appointment of a chairman I appointed a chairman. The hearings began but quickly broke down. Hon. members will recall that within a matter of hours of the breakdown of negotiations in early May of last year I was able to persuade the man I regarded as best equipped to mediate the situation to step in. I refer to Judge Lippe. He knew the problems and he had acted in a similar situation in 1963, at which time he had done an outstanding job.
Judge Lippe took this job on and after he had been at it a few days-this is of importance to those people who are so critical, and I am not referring to hon. members only but to the public generally-he said that the longshoremen had asked for a substantial increase in wages to be incorporated in the new agreement. He said that the employers seemed prepared to give them what they were asking for the year 1966 and that they would extend this into the year 1967 in return for an assurance of greater productivity during the second year.
Judge Lippe in his capacity as mediator worked on this dispute trying to bring about some assurance of increased productivity. When those efforts failed I, as minister, moved in again within a matter of hours of the time Judge Lippe asked me to do so. I invited the parties to come to Ottawa to see me. They met with me and others of my colleagues, and we were in session for several hours one afternoon extending into the early part of the following day. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been suggested by various hon. members that the members from the Montreal area have been somewhat silent in this debate, but the minister has pointed out that there are 10 or 12 members from the Montreal area who have been following the debate with a great deal of attention. Of course, in view of the fact that this debate was granted at the request of the opposition it was only normal and natural that we should have permitted members of the opposition to use up as much time as they required, but frankly I am rather surprised that there has not been full participation on the part of members who have pointed out the tremendous urgency of the situation that exists at the moment.
The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), the former minister of labour, who is not in his seat at the moment, emphasized the fact that his party voted against Bill C-215 which was introduced and passed by the house a year or two ago. I think that is a rather sad commentary on the the former minister of labour because if ever there was a good piece of labour legislation introduced in the House of Commons it was Bill C-215. I do not want to spend too much time bringing back to memory the situation at that time, but hon. members will recall that the ports of Montreal, Three Rivers and Quebec had been tied up by a devastating strike which threatened not only Expo and its starting date but also the very economic life of the nation.
Respecting, as this party has always done, the rights of labour in labour disputes and realizing that the public usually conceives at first that labour is to blame, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) bent over backwards to do nothing that could be interpreted by labour or by management as an infringement on their rights under the free collective bargaining process. But When it became apparent that a state of emergency did exist and that the economic life of the country was being affected, then and only then did the minister exert the type of pressure which under normal circumstances he would be reluctant to exert. This resulted in Bill C-215 which was passed by the house on division.


The only suggestion the former minister of labour had to offer was one which he makes on many occasions such as this, namely, bring all the parties together in Ottawa. I have heard this suggestion from the hon. member every time there has been labour dispute. However, I have looked at his record as minister of labour, and I may say it was an excellent one, and I found no hesitation on his part during the British Columbia ferry dispute to introduce legislation to bring that embarrassing strike to an end.
Nor did I find any reluctance on the part of the N.D.P. to bring the longshoremen's strike in Montreal to an end. As was pointed out by one of the members of the Conservative party today, a bill was introduced by the leader of the N.D.P., drafted by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), which, if it had been adopted, would have removed from labour their democratic privilege to strike. Regardless of what followed the longshoremen would have been forced back to work. But, as has been pointed out, the N.D.P. had second thoughts about the bill and withdrew it. Since there were no concrete and valid suggestions offered by the opposition, Bill C-215 came into existence and was discussed quite adequately in the house. It was the first breakthrough in the history of Canadian labour that faced up to the fact that the future of labour and management is bound up in a common cause, particularly in light of the fact that we are an exporting nation.
Strikes are rapidly becoming obsolete as a bargaining weapon. If labour is to share in the fruits of the wealth of this nation it must understand that wage increases and productivity go hand in hand. We can no longer afford the luxury of rising costs and lower productivity. This feeling is growing among responsible labour people. They know there is a direct relationship between productivity and labour, and the Picard report attempts to deal with this subject matter.
Without going into all the technicalities of the clauses, Bill C-215 was a piece of legislation which impressed on the ship owners, the shipping federation, that the men in the port of Montreal were entitled to an increase in pay, and impressed on the labour union that if the ship owners were to be able to afford increased wages, and at the same time Montreal was to remain competitive with other ports in North America, then the port of Montreal would have to produce more. There
November 24, 1967

would have to be increased productivity and labour would have to cease fighting modern technological methods. This was basically the problem at that time.
In order to establish properly what was the real cause of friction on the waterfront and what could be done to bring about increased productivity, under the authority of Bill C-215 the Minister of Labour established what is now known as the Picard commission or, more formally, the inquiry commission on the St. Lawrence ports. I think its report is a very significant document and I have read it not once but several times, as I hope most hon. members have.
I agree with labour that there are ambiguous sections in the report, and if they are ambiguous to labour I presume they must be ambiguous to management as well. If they are ambiguous to both sides in the dispute, then I think we have a moral duty to clarify the ambiguity. Therefore there should be no reluctance on the part of the minister or the government to make sure that Mr. Picard comes back and clarifies these ambiguous sections of his report. I think that by so doing he will in no way be infringing upon the collective agreement that is in existence between labour and management. If Mr. Picard clarifies what he meant in this report, then it would be up to labour and management to take advantage of the processes within the labour laws and the agreements should they not agree with his interpretation of the problems and the solutions.
I am speaking more as a Montrealer than as an assistant to the Minister of Labour. Unless labour and management in that port face up to realities the port of Montreal will dwindle into a second class port. There are too many alternate methods of shipping today for a port such as Montreal to be in a constant state of turmoil. In a country such as Canada which depends on export markets we cannot afford the luxury of management and labour wrangling every few months about wage agreements and working conditions.

By the same token it is unfair of anyone to presume that the source of friction is entirely on the labour side. Those who have read the Picard report and are familiar with longshor-ing, or those who know anything about port facilities, will realize that the basic and essential problem that causes friction in the
Labour Dispute at Montreal port of Montreal is job security. Job insecurity in the Montreal port is a greater threat to labour and management relations than it is-in Vancouver because of climatic conditions.
Longshoremen might be considered as unskilled labour, and the men are drawn, from the labouring or working class whose educational levels are perhaps quite low. With the realization that the port of Montreal is only open seven or eight months a year these people engaged in longshoring must, face the fact that there is little or no employment for them in the winter months. Professor Picard recognized this fact, and one of the basic principles of his report relates to-job security and minimum income spread over 52 weeks. This is a major breakthrough which was never touched upon by the opposition in the actions it took in respect of this problem in the port of Montreal.
Governments have for too long been satisfied simply to get the parties together on some form of wage agreement that would keep them together and create a little peace for the greater part of the two year period between collective agreements. They have never before got at the root or source of the problem. The Picard report does, and if there are areas of ambiguity they should be clarified. I think there is a moral obligation on Mr. Picard to come back from his holiday and clarify these ambiguities. That is my opinion, and it is not expressed by me as one on the side of labour any more than I am on the side of management. We cannot afford the luxury of keeping the port of Montreal closed when any day now the river will begin to freeze, with an ensuing economic impact on fruit growers, exporters and importers in this nation. This is a luxury we can no longer afford.

subtopic: LABOUR DISPUTE AT MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The Minister of Agriculture simply clarified a point, the point being that there are not tons of apples lying rotting on the wharves in the port of Montreal. This is the type of innuendo and false impression that unfortunately creeps into every debate involving labour. It is unfair to labour and in this case it is simply not true, as pointed out by the statistics presented by the Minister of Agriculture. I happen to think that if there is only one case of apples rotting in the port of Montreal that is one case too many.
4680	COMMONS
Labour Dispute at Montreal
The point I am trying to get at as a Montrealer is that the economy of the region, the province and the nation is such that we cannot afford the luxury of a work shutdown in the ports of Montreal, Vancouver, Three Rivers, Quebec or anywhere else in Canada. We must find ways and means to stabilize and continue peaceful negotiations between management and labour. The first practical, tangible and progressive step toward the eventual day when strikes will be obsolete and accepted as obsolete by both sides at the bargaining table is the Picard report, particularly when accepted by labour and management.
Labour must realize that Bill C-215 granted very substantial increases in wages. We have been criticized from all parts of the house and by private enterprise about the generosity of that settlement which has been erroneously interpreted as a forced settlement by the Prime Minister. That is not the case. An increase in the wages of employees on the waterfront of 35 per cent or 40 per cent would be insignificant to the ship owners provided the workers in turn would increase productivity in the port of Montreal, which is now far less than the productivity of other ports in Canada.
Labour must face up to these indisputable facts. If labour refuses to go along with the spirit of the Picard report because of a genuine misunderstanding of certain clauses, I suggest it would be better for them to carry on during the few remaining weeks until the port closes, under protest if necessary. Surely labour has a moral obligation to the port and the people using it who are not directly involved as management or labour in this dispute.
At the risk of being discourteous, Mr. Minister, I suggest that you should contact Mr. Picard and get him to cut his holiday short, come back and give us the benefit of his advice. That is my first suggestion.

subtopic: LABOUR DISPUTE AT MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

Mr. Picard should make his report so clear that whether or not the unions accept it there would be no difference in the opinion of the parties as to what the report is all about. If the unions did not accept it then they would be failing the spirit of Bill C-215 and accepting a pay increase under false pretenses.

There is ambiguity in the report. Let me point to the one portion regarding slings and the size of slings. Mr. Picard uses the word "reasonable". What is reasonable to the unions might be one thing but yet another to management. Management may feel that "reasonable" means all the weight that the slings and cranes can carry, but labour may suggest that this would reach the point where the operation is no longer safe or the point at which management was asking labour to triple productivity rather than double it. In any event I think Professor Picard has an obligation to come back and clarify these points. Once these points are clarified I think labour and management have an obligation to sit down together and thrash out their differences under the provisions of the bill.

speechtext: I do not intend to become involved in a dispute with my minister, and that is why I said I was speaking as a member from the Montreal area who believes we cannot afford the luxury of shutting down the port of Montreal. That is my first point. The second point is that if the shutdown is the result of a genuine misunderstanding of certain parts of the Picard report, then Mr. Picard should clarify its contents and make very clear to labour and management precisely what he meant by words such as "reasonable". After that is done management and labour should show good faith and, under the provisions of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, should appeal to the minister's department for assistance in bringing their dispute to an end. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-15, to amend the Inquiries Act.
He said: This bill, No. C-15, which would amend the Inquiries Act so as to restrict judges from acting as royal commissioners has two companion bills on the order paper, also introduced by me-C-16 to amend the Judges Act and C-89 to amend the Supreme Court Act. The three bills have a common purpose and in order to develop my argument it will be necessary to ask Your Honour's indulgence and that of the house to make brief reference to the other bills.
The basic purpose of the three bills is to uphold and strengthen the independence and impartiality of the judiciary. I believe Canada is uniquely fortunate in the calibre and integrity of those dedicated men, and regrettably too few women, who serve on the bench at all levels. Indeed, I assert with confidence that the quality of the Canadian judiciary is not surpassed by the judiciary of any other nation. None the less I believe and submit firmly to the house that the practice of appointing judges as royal commissioners, arbitrators, conciliators, referees, or to other such extra-judicial duties is detrimental to the best traditions of the bench, endangers the independence and impartiality of the judiciary and should now be stopped once and for all.
Companion Bill C-89 was drafted to achieve two purposes, first as an absolute prohibition against a justice of the Supreme Court of Canada serving as a commissioner under the Inquiries Act and, second, to prevent any such justice from undertaking any service of any nature-and I emphasize, any service of any nature-unrelated to his judicial duties, as a result of which he might become involved in political controversy.
4692	COMMONS
Inquiries Act Amendment
Companion Bill C-16 to amend the Judges Act would prevent judges from accepting any extra-judicial duties except when expressly authorized to do so by resolution of this house, or by resolution of a provincial legislature.
This Bill C-15 is designed to prevent a judge from being appointed a commissioner under the Inquiries Act without the express authority of a resolution of the House of Commons. Hon. members may wonder at this qualification. Provision for appointment of a judge as a commissioner with the express authority of a resolution of the House of Commons would enable the use of a judge in a very exceptional-and I repeat, very exceptional-case, where the Minister of Justice could satisfy the house that no damage to the judiciary could result.
Frankly, I would hope that this provision would seldom-perhaps never-be used, but I have inserted it as a precaution in case there might arise some emergency, or some other situation, where the duties of the proposed commissioner would be essentially judicial in character. I might use as illustrations, the Royal Commission on the Law of Insanity as a Defence in Criminal Cases, or the Royal Commission on Criminal Sexual Psychopaths.
The issue is not a new one. It has been debated many times in this chamber and I think it is only fair to say that hon. members, when they sit on this side of the house, seem to take a more jaundiced view of the practice than when they assume administrative responsibilities on the other side of the house. That distinguished and amiable scholar, Professor John C. Courtney, in a well documented article entitled "Judges as Royal Commissioners" in the winter issue, 1964-65, of the Dalhousie Review, pointed out that as early as 1872 a resolution was introduced into this house to the effect that payments received by judges for extra-judicial work "are calculated to impair the independence of the judiciary and are in contravention of the spirit of our laws designed to secure the independence of the judges". Ninety-five years later, I subscribe fully to those words.
A number of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada have in the past become embroiled in political controversy as a result of serving as royal commissioners. The greatest Canadian jurist of all time, Sir Lyman P. Duff, twice became the centre of partisan controversy as a result of his services, first as royal commissioner on transportation and second as royal commissioner on the Hong

Kong expedition. The violent attacks upon him were not, I submit, good for our highest court or for the status and prestige of our highest judicial office.

I might express this perhaps more vigorously, except that I want to bury past follies.
The best statement of this problem may be found at page 445 of Norman Ward's edition of Dawson's "The Government of Canada", from which I would quote:
There would seem to be little purpose in taking elaborate care to separate the judge from politics and to render him quite independent of the executive, and then placing him in a position as a royal commissioner where his impartiality may be attacked and his findings-no matter how correct and judicial they may be-are liable to be interpreted as favouring one political party at the expense of the other. For many of the inquiries or boards place the judge in a position where he cannot escape controversy: he may be making decisions which at least touch on policy; he may be considering, or conciliating, or deciding disputes on labour questions; he may be investigating and interrogating by very questionable procedures persons suspected of treasonable activities; he may be conducting inquiries on definitely political matters such as the Hong Kong or Bren gun charges.
It has been proved time and again that in many of these cases the judge loses in dignity and in reputation, and his future usefulness is appreciably lessened thereby. Moreover, if the judge remains away from his regular duties for long periods, he is apt to lose his sense of balance and detachment; and he finds that the task of getting back to normal and of adjusting his outlook and habits of mind to purely judicial work is by no means easy.
Basically, sir, the objections as they are stated there to extra-judicial duties are threefold; first the possibility, and in many cases the probability of a judge becoming involved in public and oft-times partisan controversy; second, that judicial work suffers-no one can moonlight without affecting his regular work, and it is a truism that justice delayed is justice denied-and third, the receipt of extra pay for judicial moonlighting is an infringement upon the independence of the bench. I am not by any means certain that the legislation passed at the last session of this parliament has solved that latter problem.
November 24, 1967	COMMONS DEBATES
All these facts were clearly pointed out by the Chief Justice of Quebec, Hon. Lucien Tremblay, in a vigorous speech to the Conference of United States Chief Justices, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of August 5, 1966, from which I quote:
Quebec's Chief Justice, Lucien Tremblay, yesterday vigourously assailed government practice of appointing judges to commissions of inquiry and labour relations boards.
Chief Justice Tremblay charged that the practice-which he termed "bad as a general rule"- delayed the course of justice, resulted in violations of the law and often misled the public.
Then later on:
"The function of a judge is to hear cases and render judgment, but when a judge gives his opinion on any other than a legal question, his opinion is not worth more than that of any other citizen of equal standing", he said.
I think perhaps I should point out to the house that the former minister of justice, Hon. Lucien Cardin, wrote to all the chief justices across Canada in July, 1966, drawing attention to sections 37 and 38 of the Judges Act, and he added:
I should appreciate it if you would draw these provisions to the attention of the judges of your court, and point out that in all cases where they propose to undertake extra-judicial duties in labour matters for private persons the consent of the governor in council must be obtained. You might also indicate that I would not be prepared to recommend to the governor in council that such consent be granted unless I am assured by you that the duties can be undertaken without interfering with the administration of justice.
Now, sir, enforcement of the requirement that a judge must have the consent of his chief justice as well as the approval of the governor in council presumably will safeguard against court proceedings suffering due to judicial absenteeism, but it does not meet the problem of public controversy or infringement of the independence of the judiciary. I have very grave doubts whether the procedures outlined by the former minister of justice are in fact being adopted and enforced, and particularly at the county and district court level. I doubt if all the Ontario county judges who have engaged in labour relations work since July, 1966, have had the approval of the governor in council.
Moonlighting by judges in the field of industrial relations has been a very genuine problem in the province of Ontario. Until the legislation of a year ago there were a few county judges in Ontario to whom the regular judicial emoluments were mere bread and butter, whereas they earned their honey and jam by supplementing their judicial earnings
Inquiries Act Amendment two or three times over through fees charged in industrial relations conciliation and arbitration work. Has this been solved completely by the new legislation? I am not by any means sure. In fact I believe it has not.
Are these outside earnings a threat to judicial independence? Personally I am satisfied that they have that potential. Judges are only human; their lofty positions do not insulate them from the frailties and temptations which beset lesser mortals. I adopt the words of a very great Canadian, a man who was an outstanding parliamentarian, a great barrister and former President of the Canadian Bar Association, John T. Hackett, later Senator Hackett, spoken in this house on June 21, 1946, as reported in Hansard at page 2709 for that date:
To the extent that these tasks are paid for, they are subversive of the principle of independence which is the bedrock of our whole judicial system. If a judge is to receive remuneration in excess of his statutory compensation, which has been horribly inadequate for generations, he is beholden to the party paying him, be it the political party in power or be it a labour union or employer who commands his services. But if the practice in the form to which I have just alluded is reprehensible, it becomes more objectionable when judges undertake tasks highly pigmented by politics.
It is impolitic for a practising barrister to say anything which might be construed as criticism of the bench. It is most unfortunate that stem necessity imposes on me the duty of pointing out the dangers to the greatest of our institutions inherent in this practice. I do not accuse the government in power of being the sole offender, but circumstances have made it the most frequent and the most recent offender-
I say with sorrow that the reputation for impartiality, dignity and honour enjoyed by the bench has been exposed to criticism by this practice. All who believe in the law, who depend upon its fearless administration, and admit that the people at large must have complete faith in the integrity of the judiciary, must oppose the continuance of this practice.
Then Mr. Hackett, after referring to labour disputes, went on:
At the present time, in the clubs, in the marketplace, wherever men meet and discuss, one hears a judge classified as "favourable to labour," another as "favourable to the interests," another as "weak and not knowing exactly which side he is on".
Those words are as wise and as true today as they were 21 years ago when they were first uttered. Equally wise and pertinent quotations could be found in numerous speeches on this subject made by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), particularly when he was the hon. gentleman from Lake Centre.
November 24, 1967

Inquiries Act Amendment
There is a further aspect, namely the assumption by judges of administrative duties. In this I am thinking particularly of judges serving on police commissions. The constitution of police commissions is a matter for the provinces, but the duties of judges, I submit, are within the jurisdiction of this parliament, and I believe parliament should prohibit judges from undertaking police commission duty. To adopt the words of Chief Justice Tremblay, "The function of a judge is to hear cases and render judgment." He should not be closer to the police than to the criminal. He should be insulated equally from both. Personally I do not believe that any judge actually achieves any bias by reason of serving on a police commission, but I do know that members of the public suspect such bias. This is an instance, surely, where the old rule applies: that justice must not only be done, it must appear to be done.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I do not suggest for a moment that the need for the types of skills which judges are alleged to possess can be left in a vacuum. From time to time royal commissions are needed, though I confess to believing that the less often the better. Certainly adjudicators, arbitrators, conciliators and referees are an essential part of modern life, and not merely in the field of industrial relations. From what segment of the population may such persons be drawn if not from the judiciary? Personally I believe they must be drawn from the academic and the practising profession. I go further and suggest that a new and trained profession in this field is now a necessity. Perhaps we could learn from France.
A former attorney general of Ontario, A. Kelso Roberts, sought to meet this problem by legislation to establish a new group of scholarly people to be known as "approved impartial referees and arbitrators". Apart from the tongue-twisting name, the idea was a good one-the establishment of a panel of qualified, yet non-judicial, referees, arbitrators, conciliators and adjudicators. The panel would achieve their status through licensing by a board of supervisors and would be available for such duties as are now performed in this field by judges. The legislation, which is chapter 5 of the statutes of Ontario of 1962, received royal assent on April 18 of that year, but regrettably has never been proclaimed. What might have been a valuable experiment has never been tried. For myself, I accept the general principles of this Ontario legislation. A system of


qualifying a new group of conciliators, arbitrators and other such persons as an alternative to bringing judges down off their benches must in my view be worked out.
What I would ask the house to do now is to send the judges back to the high and lofty status to which they were summoned; to prevent them from becoming involved in political controversy; to stop some of them from competing with one another in a money grubbing operation to see who can land the most labour relations work, and to free them from administration and give them time and opportunity for scholarship and judicial meditation. In short, let judges be judges.
In my enthusiasm for reform I may perhaps have seemed to reflect upon our bench in Canada. My dear old friend, the late John T. Hackett, said as I quoted earlier that "it is impolitic for a practising barrister to say anything which might be construed as criticism of the bench". I think it is even more impolitic for one, who has been forced by parliamentary circumstances-to his great regret-to become a non-practising barrister to appear to so criticize. For that reason I close on the note upon which I began. My admiration for the scholarship, the integrity and the independence of our Canadian judiciary is genuine and sincere. I want them to be judges in the great traditions, both of the civil and common law, and to cease being as they now are, jacks-of-all trades.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JUDGES TO SERVE AS COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always marvel at the fluent and able way the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) introduces either a private members bill or anything else in this house. I agree with many of the allegations the hon. member has made, especially in respect of the quality of the Canadian judiciary. I know of no country anywhere in the world where the judiciary is held in higher esteem. Unlike my hon. friend, it is my feeling that inquiries under the Inquiries Act are as important as any case, and sometimes they involve matters of such serious public concern the decision of a judge is more readily accepted than a decision by anyone else, because of the independence and unbiased quality our judges possess.
The hon. member for Carleton made many objections and I do not intend now to cover them entirely. He referred to the possibility of a judge becoming involved in public controversy. I suppose a judge could always become involved in public controversy but, as I will suggest in a very few minutes, there
November 24, 1967	COMMONS
are other amendments which I feel are much more important to keep judges away from such controversy.
The hon. member also mentioned that justice is sometimes delayed. It is my submission that an inquiry can be just as important as any other case, and sometimes much more important. I do not intend to deal specifically with the hon. member's third objection, but I will refer to it indirectly in a few minutes. The hon. member suggested that when a judge gives his opinion in respect of any case, other than a legal case, his opinion is worth no more than that of anyone else. Let me refer him to his opening words which can be used to refute that statement, because it is the reputation for independence and impartiality that judges possess which makes their opinion much better in a particular field than that of an ordinary person.
The hon. member referred to moonlighting in respect of industrial relations. Certainly in labour arbitration I believe that the opinions of judges are usually accepted more readily by the parties involved than by any other group of people. The hon. member suggested the reputation of impartiality may be damaged because of added remuneration. I think that equally wise quotations could be obtained regarding the value of obtaining the services of an unbiased, impartial judge.
My hon. friend mentioned that justice must not only be done, but that it must manifestly appear to be done. I am in total agreement with that statement. This is a quotation that has long been used in reference to our system of British justice. The member speaks of a new and trained profession that is needed, namely the establishment of a panel of qualified arbitrators. I would be in complete agreement if that new profession were already established, but to date that is not the case. I can only ask the hon. member whether it might be better to pass legislation setting up such an alternative before leaving us in a vacuum by preventing judges from performing this very important task.
I support the hon. member in respect of two things, and I commend him for bringing this important matter to the attention of the house. This is something which has been discussed for some time by the members of the profession which the hon. member and I share outside this house. I share his feeling that the law should be amended, but the areas of amendment in my opinion are different.
DEBATES	4695
Inquiries Act Amendment
Let me make two points in this regard. Under the Inquiries Act the terms of reference for the commissioners should be submitted to this house. It is very important that the terms of reference be fair. In my short time in the house I have heard discussions on at least one, if not two occasions, about terms of reference, so far as certain members of this house were concerned, not being exactly fair. They should be fair and perhaps one way of making sure they are fair would be by submitting them to this house for approval.
My second point is that the commissioner should be restricted to findings of fact, and should not pass judgment on those facts. That responsibility should be left to the house. In other words, the facts found by the commissioner should be presented to the house, where any judgment on the basis of those facts should be made. I do not intend to deal with any of the commissions of late but would just give this example. Let us suppose it is alleged that a minister did not use good judgment in entering into a contract. Pursuant to the provisions of an order in council, a judge is appointed a commissioner under part I of the Inquiries Act to inquire into whether the minister used good judgment in entering into the contract. The commissioner should inquire into the facts, as for example whether other tenders were called and the circumstances surrounding the contract.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
When the judge, acting as a commissioner, makes a finding of fact, parliament should then make the judgment on those facts. In other words, it is for parliament to decide on the facts whether the conduct of the minister was open to censure. The judge should be relieved of passing judgment on a minister or member of parliament on any matter relating to the responsibilities of a member of this house. If a commissioner decides only on the facts, I submit he will not be exposed in the way in which the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has very carefully pointed out on so many occasions.
I should like to discuss for a moment only one of the examples put forward so ably by the hon. member for Carleton. I refer to the commission that was set up to report on the Hong Kong expedition. As the hon. member for Carleton said, Chief Justice Lyman Duff was appointed the royal commissioner in that
4696
November 24, 1967

Inquiries Act Amendment case to inquire into the organization, authorization and despatch of the Canadian expeditionary force to Hong Kong in October, 1941.
I quote from the report by the royal commissioner:
The order in council states that the purpose of the investigation is to determine whether there occurred any dereliction of duty or error in judgment by those whose duty it was to arrange for the authorization, organization and despatch of the force that resulted in detriment or injury to the expedition or its members.
I am not reading this out just for the sake of reading it. I would like to cite this case to the hon. member for Carleton as an example of how we can take the law as it exists today and use it by submitting only facts to the commissioner involved. In making a finding of fact the commissioner could not possibly, in my respectful submission, be exposed in the way put forward by the hon. member for Carleton. Later in his report the commissioner said:
My duty is to determine whether there occurred any dereliction of duty or error in judgment "on the part of any of the personnel or of any of the departments of the government whose duty it was to arrange for the authorization, organization and despatch of the expeditionary force"-
If a finger can be raised against the commissioner in this particular case, it is the terms of reference that are responsible and not the commissioner himself. The commissioner went on to say in the report:
-and whether, if such dereliction or error occurred, there resulted detriment or injury to the expedition or the troops comprising it.
Five points are set out by the commissioner in his report but I will summarize those which can be taken as factual matters. First, who authorized the expedition? That is fine as far as it goes. This refers to the expedition that left Canada on October 27, 1941.
On page 4 of the report the commissioner pointed out one thing that I should like to bring to the attention of the house. As far as I can see, this is the only time in the report when he expressed an opinion, but in my respectful submission this opinion was expressed because of the terms of reference themselves. He said:
It would perhaps be a possible view that the propriety of this decision by the government is exclusively a matter for consideration and discussion by parliament.
In expressing that view it would seem the commissioner felt he was making a finding of fact and it would be up to parliament to decide, on the facts, whether there had

occurred any dereliction of duty, rather than it being left to the commissioner to himself find that dereliction.
In this connection I should like to stress to the hon. member for Carleton that if the commissioner had to make up his mind only on matters of fact, all the objections upon which he based his bill and which he mentioned in his speech today would be completely superfluous. The commissioner went on to say:
Since, however, I am required to pass upon the question, it is my duty to say that I have no doubt the course taken by the government was the only course open to them in the circumstances.
Of course, there is one advantage in having it done that particular way. As I mentioned, there were certain secret documents and telegrams here that probably would not have been exposed to this house. Second, the commissioner had to deal with the question of the selection of the units for the expeditionary force. That was a factual matter. In that case the minister could easily have found on that point of fact without any criticism from anyone. Third, he had to consider the steps taken to bring the units up to strength, including first reinforcements; fourth, the general organization and despatch of the force, apart from the subject of mechanical transport; and fifth, mechanical transport-that is, the number of vehicles, and so on. If all those five matters were decided by the commissioner, I would say to the hon. member for Carleton that no criticism could be placed on him. Of course, I agree with the commissioner's findings in that case; but if the facts alone had been left to the commissioner, and those facts brought back to this house for judgment, it would have left the commissioner in a much better position.
It is often mentioned in the house that parliament is too busy to deal with matters of this kind. At no time has this been quite as obvious as it was in the last few days. I am not going to give all the examples that I could, but in the debate on capital punishment the other day the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) said, as reported in Hansard at page 4261:
There are also many very urgent matters which the house should be considering.
The hon. member for Prince Edward-Len-nox (Mr. Alkenbrack) said on the same day, as reported at page 4281 of Hansard:
-despite the serious economic ills which now beset our country and the need for useful and
November 24, 1967	COMMONS
beneficial legislation concerning economic matters, the government now wastes the time of parliament by sponsoring this bill dealing with the Criminal Code, which will be productive of nothing of benefit to Canada.
The next day the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) spoke of impending legislation and said there were other ways in which this house could be more gainfully and more usefully employed, and that it was no time to debate a bill that would bring about changes to the Criminal Code. It has been said on many occasions that parliament is so busy. I would ask the hon. member for Carleton whether parliament is not too busy to discuss and take up the time necessary in dealing with his bill.

No, Mr. Speaker, I am merely pointing out what would happen if this amendment became law. Unless the governor in council were expressly authorized in a particular case to appoint a commissioner by resolution of the House of Commons, it would mean that every time a commissioner was appointed by resolution of the house the matter would have to be discussed.
I listened to a debate in this house not too long ago about terms of reference, and I hate to think of 265 members expressing their views about a particular judge or judges named in a resolution to do a job required by the government. I submit it would be a very lengthy discussion.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It is obvious that if the names of judges are bandied about and if an extended discussion concerning judges is carried on in the house, this would not add to the dignity, unbiased nature and reputation which judges and courts possess in Canada at this time.
I should like to say a few words about judges. They have a great security of tenure in Canada. Their appointments last until they reach the age of 75 years. It is an established practice in Canada not to lower the salaries of judges; so their future is assured. The executive cannot say to a judge "If you do not do "a certain thing", your salary will be cut down to $1 a year", which, all in all, makes them very independent. Over the years they have built up a tradition of impartiality and objectivity. People in Canada respect their independence. What my hon.
DEBATES	4697
Inquiries Act Amendment friend said to sum up the reputation of judges in this country cannot be expressed in a better way. The reputation enjoyed by the judges also applies to the courts.
I have already covered one difficulty of appointing judges by a resolution, namely that it would take much time of parliament to discuss and criticize the personalities of the judges. The airing of this subject would destroy the respect which the public has for judges today. If that were to happen, we would also lose respect for the law. The judges themselves would be the subject of an inquiry before the inquiry ever took place, and after such a public inquiry in the house the public would not be prepared to accept the finding of the commissioner. In my respectful submission it would be a retrograde step which would undermine one of our most viable institutions, namely our judges and our courts.

Mr. Speaker, in my view the bill which the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has introduced, with his usual eloquence, undoubtedly points to a problem which exists and which is real. I am not at all certain, however, that the bill offers a solution, and perhaps that is the consideration which should be uppermost in our minds when we assess a proposal of this kind. If I heard the hon. member correctly, he was quoting another opinion when he argued that court proceedings were suffering from judicial absenteeism, and he spent some time discussing what he referred to as judicial moonlighting. For a while I hesitated in deciding whether or not I should inject myself into this discussion, because I do not have knowledge in the operation of the courts which is possessed by someone in the profession of the hon. member for Carleton. But on second thought I decided that I would take part in the discussion because perhaps the hon. member's search for a solution may be restricted and limited by the special knowledge he has in this field, and which I lack.
Both he and the hon. member who followed him expressed some concern that the integrity and the honour in which courts in this land are held should not in any way be impaired. The hon. member for Carleton argued that as a result of some of the activities in which members of the judiciary are called upon to engage there is a lowering of their reputation in the minds of the people of this country. In my view these activities,
November 24, 1967

Inquiries Act Amendment which tend to lower our faith in the integrity of the judiciary, which faith we all consider to be desirable, have not been activities under the Inquiries Act but have rather resulted from certain defects in the laws. I might as well say at once that I am referring to certain applications for injunctions which are becoming increasingly frequent in our society.
I think that probably most members of the house would agree that the fact that judges are being called upon to perform functions which are outside their traditional duties indicates that there is a need in our society for people to perform these tasks with the integrity and detachment which we traditionally associate with the judiciary. Therefore I suggest for the consideration of the house that instead of the proposal made by the hon. member for Carleton, which would in effect prohibit the use of judges under the Inquiries Act, except in some rare instances, and because of the very reasons that were advanced by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Stafford) that no government will wish to have frequent debates in the house regarding the appointment of judges under the Inquiries Act, we should consider expanding our traditional view of the courts. It seems to me from a layman's point of view, that our judicial system and the decision as to the number of judges which we appoint, was established in the context of a much simpler society which, by and large, was rural. At that time the only need for people in such a detached position was in cases involving civil or criminal actions; whereas in our present society there is an increasing need for judges presiding over inquiries going far beyond the scope of the traditional courts. Perhaps we should therefore think of an expansion of the whole concept of what is involved in being a judge.
The hon. member for Carleton suggested that we should think of employing in this capacity academics and other professionals. I suggest to him that academics have knowledge in a special field, whereas there is a need for someone who is beyond and above any particular specialty and who is in a position to assess and to judge certain cases. In many instances the matters that are being dealt with are of such broad public interest that the persons appointed to deal with them must enjoy the prestige and impartiality normally required in carrying out the functions of a court.


[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
There have been of course many suggestions for the setting up of panels of arbitrators or referees. I have been wondering whether or not any action we might take in this parliament would be likely to attract or develop a group in our society which would have anything like the prestige traditionally associated in the minds of citizens with judges. I have been wondering whether or not we should take a different approach to certain appointments in order to provide panels of people on the bench from whom we could draw for this very important social purpose, rather than have these judges haggling over some civil action.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that I have the answer to this problem. However, I believe some such approach as I have suggested might be sounder than the bill proposed by the hon. member for Carleton which, in a sense, is going to restrict the availability of competent people, with the prestige that is required to do very necessary jobs in our society, without putting anyone else in their place. I suggest to the hon. member for Carleton that he put his fertile imagination to work on a proposal which might appeal to more of us, and bring about a desirable solution to the important problem we have in which our judges admittedly have been caught up in a rather unfortunate way.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JUDGES TO SERVE AS COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
We
have had very learned addresses on this private bill from the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) and from the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Stafford). I think the hon. member for Elgin has successfully demolished the argument of the sponsor of the bill. There is one aspect of this subject that has not been dealt with, Mr. Speaker, and that is that if we are going effectively to limit judges from serving as royal commissioners, then we must of course ask where we can find others to do this work. The purpose of a royal commission is to get a number of different views. By appointing three, five or seven persons to a royal commission you would get these different views and then, by a process of distillation of opinion, the royal commissioners reach a consensus on some important social or economic problem which they have been asked to examine.
We must ask ourselves, who would replace the judges? The first group of people that come to mind would be the economists. It is said of economists that if you put three in a
November 24, 1967

room you get four opinions. If we made up a royal commission of economists, the taxpayers would get one opinion for nothing, so I think that would be a desirable saving to the taxpayers.
After giving the matter more thought, it seemed to me that if we were not going to allow judges to sit on royal commissions we should perhaps have royal commissions made up of newspaper publishers and editors. It seems to me there are a number of important benefits from this proposal. Of course if a royal commission were made up of newspaper publishers, we would be assured from the beginning that the royal commission would have the benefit of a wide range of views on any given subject into which the commission inquired. If one picks ten editorials on any given subject, he usually finds there are three editors in favour, three opposed, two editors usually have not decided on their position, and by the end of the editorial two more have managed not to declare themselves either for or against. Therefore, we have the advantage of being automatically guaranteed a wide range of opinion.
It seems to me therefore it would be very good for newspaper publishers and editors to be appointed royal commissioners. They would have to grapple with the problems of the nation, rather than sit in their offices and write editorials. This would be a good training for them. A more important benefit is that we would be automatically guaranteed editorial support for whatever recommendations the royal commission might make. As it is now, we have recommendations coming from royal commissions which cost us a great deal of money, and then the newspaper publishers across the country set about shooting down those recommendations in flames. If the recommendations were made by the publishers, then automatically when the royal commission report was made public it would receive the overwhelming support of the Canadian editorial writers. The recommendations would then be easily implemented by the government. I think we could solve the major issues of the nation in this way.
I suggest, for example, a royal commission on foreign ownership might be composed of the publishers of the Toronto Star, the Winnipeg Free Press and the Vancouver Sun. Perhaps the Edmonton Journal could be included. They would sit down and analyse this question, then come out with a royal commission report on foreign ownership
Inquiries Act Amendment which I am sure would solve the problem once and for all. Perhaps we could have a royal commission on French-English relations composed of the publisher of the Orillia Packet, the Vancouver Province and Le Devoir. I am sure they would solve this problem once and for all. When these commissioners made their recommendations they would have unanimous editorial support across the country, and we could implement their recommendations without further controversy. Then we could get on with the other problems of the nation.
We could have, for example, a royal commission on economic prospects and policy, composed of the publishers of the Halifax Chronicle, the Toronto Telegram and the Winnipeg Tribune. In this way, we could have a consensus on what we should be doing about inflation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) could implement the report of the royal commission and receive newspaper support right across the country.
